title: Obfuscated Files or Information: LNK Icon Smuggling
shortTitle: Obfuscated Files or Information: LNK Icon Smuggling
summary: LNK icon smuggling abuses a Windows shortcut file so that a remote address rides along inside what looks like a harmless image path. A shortcut is a small metadata container with several data blocks, and one of them, the icon location block, tells Explorer where to fetch a picture to display for the file. That field accepts a network path or Universal Naming Convention (UNC) location, so opening a folder that contains the shortcut can cause the workstation to reach out and pull a file from an attacker controlled host. The download happens through the shell rather than through a scripting engine, which lets the traffic blend with ordinary network file access, and the same shortcut can pair the icon path with a target command so that the fetched content is then executed by a scripting interpreter or a trusted system binary. The shortcut may arrive as a phishing attachment or be created on an already compromised host to pull down follow-on tooling. Defenders spot it through shortcut parsing, file system auditing of shortcut creation, and network monitoring that flags SMB or WebDAV (Web Distributed Authoring and Versioning) requests from workstations to unfamiliar hosts outside normal business patterns.

beginner.definition: LNK icon smuggling means hiding a download command inside a Windows shortcut file. A shortcut is the small file that points to a program or folder when you double click it. Shortcuts store the web or network address of the picture they show as their icon. An attacker can put their own address in that field. This is a sub-technique of Obfuscated Files or Information.
beginner.whyItMatters: Shortcut files look harmless to most users and to many email filters. The download uses normal file sharing, so it can look like ordinary network traffic. Simply opening the folder that holds the shortcut can start the connection. The same shortcut can then run the file it downloaded. This makes a small, overlooked file into a working delivery method.
howItWorks: The attacker edits a shortcut file so that its icon points to a host they control.
Because the field supports network paths, the value can be a remote share address.
The shortcut is delivered by email, chat or a shared folder, often named like a document.
When the user opens the folder, Explorer reads the icon field to draw the picture.
The computer connects out and fetches the file from the attacker's location.
The target field of the shortcut can then run that file through a script or system tool.
beginner.example: Think of a courier who delivers a parcel based only on the return address label. A resident leaves a note saying the parcel should be fetched from a certain depot before delivery. Someone rewrites that depot address to a stranger's warehouse. The courier follows the label, collects a package from the stranger and brings it inside the building. Nobody checked the note against a trusted list, because it was just a note on the door.
takeaways: Treat any shortcut file that references a remote network location as suspicious.
Watch workstation connections to file sharing or web authoring shares that are not normal business traffic.
Check what a shortcut actually points to, including its icon path, before users open it.

objectives: Explain how the icon location field of a Windows shortcut can be abused to fetch a remote file.
Describe why shell based downloads blend with ordinary network file traffic more easily than scripted ones.
Identify artefacts such as recent shortcut creation, icon environment data blocks and outbound share connections.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent obfuscation technique and from HTML smuggling.
Describe the hunting steps you would take after a suspicious shortcut appears on a workstation.
